newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Separatist chief on first visit to Georgia capital.
newsitem.headline: Separatist chief on first visit to Georgia capital.

text.p: Vladislav Ardzinba, leader of Georgia's breakaway Abkhazia region, arrived in the capital Tbilisi on Thursday for unprecedented face-to-face peace talks with President Eduard Shevardnadze.
Ardzinba arrived with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov amid heavy security at the city's airport. Primakov's visit was previously announced but Ardzinba's presence was a surprise.

They were immediately driven to Shevardnadze's Krtsanisi residence in the hills above the city. Shevardnadze and Ardzinba, bitter enemies since the 1992-93 conflict between Georgians and Abkhaz in which about 10,000 people were killed, briefly hugged before beginning face-to-face talks.

Ardzinba's visit is the first to Georgia since he became leader of Abkhazia and took place five years to the day since Georgian troops entered the province to try to halt its moves towards independence.

"Russia is doing everything to end this conflict which has taken the lives of so many people," Primakov told reporters before talks started. "Those who think that Russia is not doing enough are mistaken. Let's hope everything will be successful."

Primakov said that he would join in the talks only after the direct session between Ardzinba and Shevardnadze, who is a former Soviet foreign minister. Primakov called Ardzinba's visit "a big step in itself".
Talks between Georgia and Abkhazia on reaching a full political agreement have been deadlocked and the latest round of U.N.-mediated negotiations has produced no tangible results.
The subtropical Black Sea region has run itself as a de facto independent state since the war.
No state has recognised Abkhazia and Western diplomats and U.N. officials have told separatist leaders that there is no prospect any will.

Abkhazia is one of several bloody conflicts which have bedeviled Georgia since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. Shevardnadze, humiliated by the loss of what many consider the most beautiful and richest part of the country, sees his role in Georgian history as recovering the province.
Shevardnadze has compared his task to that of David the Builder, an 11th century king who united Georgia's bickering mountain princedoms.
Primakov has said he hopes to prepare a deal between Georgia and Abkhazia to pave the way for a formal peace agreement to be signed in Moscow in the presence of President Boris Yeltsin.

Yeltsin has recently supported the Georgian position that Abkhazia should be part of Georgia but receive wide autonomy, and that the separatist government should allow at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees to return to their homes.
Abkhazia wants a type of "union state" confederation. This has been repeatedly rejected by Tbilisi.
Russia also has 1,500 peacekeepers in a buffer zone between Abkhazia and Georgia.

The mandate for the Russian force expired on July 31 but they will stay in the zone until their fate can be decided by the leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) which groups 12 former Soviet republics in September.
A possible withdrawal of the contingent has stirred concern among political analysts, who say it would probably spark new bloodshed.

Georgia wants the peacekeepers to police more of Abkhazia and help resettle refugees. Commonwealth leaders approved the changes earlier this year but Russia has refused to take them up, citing Abkhaz objections.
Shevardnadze has urged Moscow not to ease sanctions against Abkhazia imposed two years ago by the CIS leaders.

A partial sea blockade, enforced almost entirely by Russian naval vessels, and strict restrictions on movement through the region's only land border with Russia have crippled Abkhazia's once thriving tourist-driven economy.
